author: high6
claim: All subgoals of the Hall induction plan are solved; the plan yields a complete self-contained proof.
evidence: Necessity: matched partners of S are |S| distinct vertices of N(S). Sufficiency: induct on n=|X|. For n=0 use the empty matching. If a nonempty proper A has |N(A)|=|A|, induction gives a matching of A into N(A). On the complementary graph with left class X\A and right class Y\N(A), every T has neighborhood N(T)\N(A), whose size is at least |T| by applying Hall to A union T and subtracting |N(A)|=|A|; induction gives a second matching, and their union saturates X. If no such A exists and n>0, Hall gives an edge xy. Delete x and y. For every nonempty T subset X\{x}, T is proper in X and hence |N(T)|>=|T|+1; deletion of y lowers its neighborhood size by at most one. The empty T is automatic. Induction gives a matching saturating X\{x}; adjoining xy saturates X.

links.attempt_summary: Both implications and both induction cases close.

glossary.A: a nonempty proper subset of X
glossary.T: a subset of the complementary left class

author: high2
claim: The full Hall marriage theorem is solved by strong induction on |X|, using a tight-subset split when one exists and deletion of an adjacent pair when every proper nonempty subset has positive slack.
evidence: Assume the Hall inequalities. Induct on n=|X|. For n=0 use the empty matching. For n>0, if some nonempty proper A subset X satisfies |N(A)|=|A|, the induced graph on A and N(A) satisfies Hall and hence has, by induction, a matching saturating A. In the induced residual graph on X\A and Y\N(A), for every T subset X\A, Hall on A union T gives |A|+|T| <= |N(A union T)| = |N(A)|+|N(T)\N(A)|, so |N(T)\N(A)| >= |T|. Induction gives a matching saturating X\A; the two matchings have disjoint vertex sets and combine. If no nonempty proper A is tight, integer cardinalities give |N(A)| >= |A|+1 for each such A. Choose x in X and y in N({x}), which is nonempty by Hall. Delete x and y. Every nonempty T subset X\{x} is proper in X, so its new neighborhood has size at least |N(T)|-1 >= |T|. Induction yields a matching of X\{x}; adjoining xy saturates X. The reverse implication is the injection from each subset S into its distinct matched neighbors.

author: high7
claim: Subgoal solved: if a nonempty proper tight set A subsetneq X satisfies |N(A)|=|A|, Hall's condition splits into two smaller instances whose matchings combine.
evidence: Let H be induced on A union N(A). For B subseteq A, every G-neighbor of B lies in N(A), so N_H(B)=N_G(B) and |N_H(B)|>=|B|. Let K be induced on (X\A) union (Y\N(A)). For B subseteq X\A, N_K(B)=N_G(B)\N(A), and N_G(A union B) is the disjoint union of N(A) and N_K(B). Therefore |A|+|N_K(B)|=|N_G(A union B)|>=|A union B|=|A|+|B|, so K also satisfies Hall. Both left classes are smaller than X. Inductively obtain matchings saturating A in H and X\A in K. Their left and right vertex sets are disjoint, so their union is a matching saturating X.

evidence: Assume G satisfies Hall's inequalities and A is a nonempty proper subset of X with |N(A)|=|A|. Induction gives a matching saturating X\A. The two graphs have disjoint vertex classes, so the union of their matchings saturates X.

author: high7
claim:
Let (G=(X\sqcup Y,E)) be a finite bipartite graph. For (S\subseteq X), let

\[
N(S)=\{y\in Y: \text{(y) is adjacent to at least one vertex of (S)}\}.
\]

Prove that (G) has a matching saturating every vertex of (X) if and only if

\[
|N(S)|\ge |S|
\]

for every subset (S\subseteq X).
evidence:
First suppose that \(M\) is a matching saturating \(X\). For an arbitrary \(S\subseteq X\), let \(f(x)\) be the endpoint in \(Y\) of the unique edge of \(M\) incident with \(x\), for each \(x\in S\). Then \(f(x)\in N(S)\). If \(x,x'\in S\) are distinct, the matching edges incident with them cannot have the same endpoint in \(Y\), so \(f(x)\ne f(x')\). Thus \(f:S\to N(S)\) is injective, and finiteness implies \(|S|\le |N(S)|\).

Conversely, suppose that \(|N(S)|\ge |S|\) for every \(S\subseteq X\). We prove that \(G\) has a matching saturating \(X\) by induction on \(n=|X|\).

If \(n=0\), the empty matching saturates \(X\). Now let \(n\ge 1\), and assume the assertion has been proved for every finite bipartite graph whose left bipartition class has cardinality smaller than \(n\).

Case 1: there is a nonempty proper subset \(A\subsetneq X\) with \(|N(A)|=|A|\). Let \(H\) be the subgraph of \(G\) induced by \(A\cup N(A)\), with left class \(A\) and right class \(N(A)\). For every \(B\subseteq A\), every neighbor in \(G\) of a vertex of \(B\) belongs to \(N(A)\), because \(B\subseteq A\). Hence the neighborhood \(N_H(B)\) of \(B\) in \(H\) is exactly \(N(B)\), and therefore \(|N_H(B)|=|N(B)|\ge |B|\). Since \(0<|A|<n\), the induction hypothesis gives a matching \(M_1\) in \(H\) saturating \(A\).

Let \(K\) be the subgraph of \(G\) induced by
\[
(X\setminus A)\cup (Y\setminus N(A)),
\]
with left class \(X\setminus A\) and right class \(Y\setminus N(A)\). Fix \(B\subseteq X\setminus A\). Its neighborhood in \(K\) is
\[
N_K(B)=N(B)\setminus N(A).
\]
Moreover,
\[
N(A\cup B)=N(A)\cup N(B)
          =N(A)\,\sqcup\,\bigl(N(B)\setminus N(A)\bigr),
\]
where the last union is disjoint. Since \(A\cap B=\varnothing\), Hall's assumed inequality applied to \(A\cup B\), together with \(|N(A)|=|A|\), gives
\[
|A|+|N_K(B)|
 =|N(A\cup B)|
 \ge |A\cup B|
 =|A|+|B|.
\]
Cancelling \(|A|\) yields \(|N_K(B)|\ge |B|\). The left class \(X\setminus A\) has cardinality smaller than \(n\), so the induction hypothesis gives a matching \(M_2\) in \(K\) saturating \(X\setminus A\). Every edge of \(M_1\) has its endpoints in \(A\) and \(N(A)\), while every edge of \(M_2\) has its endpoints in \(X\setminus A\) and \(Y\setminus N(A)\). Consequently \(M_1\cup M_2\) is a matching, and it saturates all of \(X\).

Case 2: no nonempty proper subset \(A\subsetneq X\) satisfies \(|N(A)|=|A|\). The assumed inequalities and integrality then imply
\[
|N(A)|\ge |A|+1
\]
for every nonempty proper subset \(A\subsetneq X\). Choose \(x\in X\). Applying the assumed inequality to \(\{x\}\) gives \(|N(\{x\})|\ge 1\), so choose \(y\in N(\{x\})\); then \(xy\in E\). Let \(G'\) be the subgraph induced by
\[
(X\setminus\{x\})\cup(Y\setminus\{y\}),
\]
with left class \(X\setminus\{x\}\). For any \(B\subseteq X\setminus\{x\}\), its neighborhood in \(G'\) is
\[
N_{G'}(B)=N(B)\setminus\{y\}.
\]
If \(B=\varnothing\), then \(|N_{G'}(B)|=0=|B|\). If \(B\ne\varnothing\), then \(B\) is a nonempty proper subset of \(X\), so
\[
|N_{G'}(B)|=|N(B)\setminus\{y\}|
\ge |N(B)|-1
\ge |B|.
\]
Thus \(G'\) satisfies Hall's inequalities. Its left class has cardinality \(n-1<n\), so the induction hypothesis gives a matching \(M'\) in \(G'\) saturating \(X\setminus\{x\}\). No edge of \(M'\) is incident with \(x\) or \(y\), so \(M'\cup\{xy\}\) is a matching saturating \(X\).

The two cases exhaust all possibilities, proving the converse and hence the equivalence.

author: high
claim: The tight-set/slack induction plan proves the full Hall marriage theorem.
evidence: Necessity maps each x in S injectively to its distinct matched neighbor. For sufficiency, induct on |X|. If a nonempty proper A has |N(A)|=|A|, induction matches A inside A union N(A). For B subseteq X\A, the residual neighborhood has size |N(A union B)|-|N(A)| >= |A|+|B|-|A|=|B|, so induction also matches X\A in Y\N(A), and the matchings unite. If no proper nonempty set is tight, every such B has |N(B)|>=|B|+1. Choose an edge xy, delete x and y; every nonempty B subseteq X\{x} loses at most one neighbor and still satisfies Hall. Induction matches X\{x}, and adding xy saturates X. The verifier accepted the complete verbatim theorem as fact 35a0e28a6cd684b9.
